summary: The article describes how sustainable and eco-friendly products moved from niche to mainstream between September 2023 and early 2024, driven by regulation, technology and generational values. It profiles businesses and tools such as GlobalCorp, Releaf, EcoChoice and SunCab that show the shift across large corporations, startups and services. It also notes challenges like upfront costs and greenwashing, and stresses consumer education.
one_line: Eco-friendly products have gone mainstream, driven by regulation, technology and younger consumers, though cost and greenwashing remain obstacles.
key_facts: Jennifer Atkinson, CEO of the Sustainable Business Network, told entrepreneurs in November 2023 that a "triple helix" of regulatory changes, technological advancements and a generational shift in values is driving the green revolution.
Millennials and Gen Z consumers show a distinct preference for brands that align with their eco-conscious values.
Emma Lopez, a small boutique owner in town, stocked her shelves with clothing made from organic cotton and recycled fabrics.
EcoChoice, an app created by tech entrepreneur Raj Singh, launched in January 2024 and gives users a quick scan of a product's sustainability score.
Lucas Dreyfuss, innovation director at GlobalCorp, says the company has reduced its manufacturing waste by 40% and aims to be carbon neutral by 2030.
Sophia Rodriguez's startup Releaf manufactures biodegradable utensils, and she says its business has tripled since last year.
SunCab, a ridehailing service launched in February 2024 by founder Amir Patel, has a fleet made up exclusively of electric vehicles.
The initial cost outlay for greener practices can be burdensome for small businesses.
Greenwashing, where companies make deceptive claims about products' eco-friendliness, is a challenge for the sustainable market.
Vanessa Yung, a sustainability consultant, says education empowers consumers to make informed choices and challenges businesses to be accountable and transparent.
Regulatory bodies worldwide have begun enacting stricter laws on waste and emissions, pushing companies to reconsider product lifecycles.
